title: Handover: Byte, the Lab, Vanil and n8n

story: Friday, 22:00. Nave, who built Byte, our review agent, and FCP Lab, the whole product running on one machine, is on a plane. At that moment every Byte review starts to fail at the same step. Byte reviews every pull request in fcp, and soon it will review every agent's draft too. Someone finds the recording of a walkthrough Nave gave last month and watches it. It explains how Byte works. It does not explain what to do when the container image that runs the reviews was never signed, and nobody but Nave has ever built or deployed Byte.

The same is true for three more tools. FCP Lab runs on every full-size agent VM, so if it breaks, every agent run stops. Vanil, Nave's compliance agent, lives in n8n, an automation tool on our internal cluster, and its workflows exist only inside n8n's database. All four have one person who can fix them.
hook.question: How do you know that someone other than the builder can really fix a tool, before the night you need them?

read.h: Put it where a second person can reach it
p: A tool that only one person can fix is a single point of failure: when that person is away, nobody can repair it. Teams call the number behind this the bus factor: how many people a project can lose before nobody can keep it running. For these four tools it is one. Before anyone else can learn a tool, the tool has to live where they can reach it. FCP Lab's repo still sits in a personal account, so it moves into the RhinoHealth org with a repository transfer, a GitHub setting that moves a repo to a new owner. GitHub redirects the old clone URLs, so nobody's laptop breaks, and the repo gets the same team access as fcp.

Vanil has no repo at all, so its workflows are exported from n8n as JSON into a new private repo. A workflow export holds the nodes, how they are connected and their settings. For a credential it holds only an id and a name, never the secret itself. That rule protects only the credentials that were created properly, though. If someone pasted a token straight into a node's settings, the export carries it in plain text. So before the first push, a scanner called gitleaks reads every file and fails when it finds something that looks like a key or a token.

notes.text: Each workflow keeps its id, so a restore brings it back under the same id.
The credential appears only as an id and a name. The secret stays in n8n's own database.

read.see:
RuleID:      github-pat
File:        /scan/vanilRedline0001.json
Line:        49
…
WRN leaks found: 1
exit 1
(gitleaks on the lab's backup: a token pasted into a node's header, caught before any push)

deeper.h: Go deeper: a backup that is itself a workflow
p: n8n's database already keeps 14 days of snapshots, but a snapshot is the whole database: you cannot read one workflow in it, review a change to it, or bring back one workflow without bringing back everything. What is missing is a readable copy in git. The plan builds it in n8n itself, as a small nightly workflow: a Schedule Trigger, then n8n's own node with the operation Workflows: Get many, then a GitHub node that writes each workflow as a file into the Vanil repo. Its GitHub token can write to that one repo only, the same narrowest-access rule as the agents' rows in the inventory.

read.h: A page for the person who did not build it
p: The second thing a new maintainer needs is a when-it-breaks page: a short runbook, which means a page of steps for a known problem, written for the person who did not build the tool and is reading it at night. It has three parts, in the order you use them. First look: the three places to check, in order. Symptoms: a table of what you see, the likely cause and the fix. Escalate: who to call, and what the failure really costs.

The page is written from real failures, not from imagination, which is why the tool's builder writes the first version and records a walkthrough next to it. Look at the last line of Byte's page. Byte is advisory: it comments on pull requests, but no rule waits for it, so while it is down, pull requests still merge with one approval. That one sentence tells a stranger at 22:00 how urgent the problem really is.

code.text:
# When Byte breaks

Owner: Nave · Second maintainer: <name> · Alerts: #byte · Dashboard: DASHBOARD.md on the telemetry branch

## First look
1. The PR's "Byte Review" check and the caller run (byte-review.yml in the PR's repo).
2. The run artifact `byte-review-*`: the result JSON and the broker audit log.
3. `runner-canary.yml`: if the daily canary is red, the runner is the problem, not Byte.

## Symptoms
| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| No review after `@byte-review` | byte-runner-set at its max (15), or the gate skipped the PR | Look at queued jobs, then the gate log |
| Every run fails at the verify step | the main image was not signed (sign job red) | Rebuild from main; never repin by hand |
| Reviews behave like a branch build | shared `BYTE_WORKER_IMAGE` left on a branch digest | Restore the production digest |
| Every run fails at the model call | the Claude credential expired or was revoked | Rotate it as docs/setup.md says (by day 330) |

## Escalate
Nave, then the second maintainer. Byte is advisory: while it is down, PRs still merge with 1 approval.

notes.text: The header names the owner, the second maintainer, where alerts arrive and where the numbers are.
Check the runner before Byte: if the daily canary job is red, the machines are broken, not Byte.
Friday's failure. The main build signs the image that runs reviews, and a check refuses an unsigned one.
The trap of testing a change on a branch: put the shared image setting back afterwards.
How urgent it is, in one sentence: Byte comments, it never blocks a merge.

p: A recording and a page are where a handover starts, not where it ends. Watching someone fix a tool does not show that you can, any more than watching a driving video shows you can drive. So the handover counts as done only when the second maintainer has shipped one small, real change to each tool, through normal review, with the builder reviewing but not driving. For Byte that means building and testing it the way its CI does (npm ci, then npm run check), trying the change on a branch image, a test image built from the branch, as Byte's README describes, putting the shared image setting back, merging, and watching the main build sign the new image. For FCP Lab it means booting a full stack with the change, reviewing it against the running stack, and merging.

The last step is the one people skip: the second maintainer corrects both pages wherever reality was different from what they said. The same rule holds for the n8n backup. A backup counts only when it has been restored somewhere it did not come from, a fresh n8n that has never seen the workflows. A proof that cannot fail is not a proof: restore a backup into the same n8n it came from, and the workflows are listed even if the backup is empty, because they were never gone.
read.see:
Successfully imported 1 workflow.
vanilSync0000001|Vanil: Vanta to Jira sync
No credentials found with specified filters
(the lab's restore into a fresh n8n: the workflow is back, and its credential is not)

deeper.h: Go deeper: the Lab's page, and the VM image as its second reader
p: FCP Lab's page has the same three parts. Its first look is the Lab's own doctor and clean commands, which show Docker memory, the machine's architecture and which stacks already hold ports and memory, and then the failing service's logs. Its symptoms are the ones people really hit: a stack that never gets healthy because another stack holds the ports, a seed step that fails after a branch changed the database migrations, an image that cannot be pulled from our package mirror, and an image built for a Mac's arm64 processor that does not exist for the x86 processors of an agent VM.

The page also has a second reader: the VM image, which has the Lab built into it. So the walkthrough lists what the image needs from the Lab, its images, its seed database and its compose files, and who to ask about each. On an agent VM, a health check stops the run before any code is written if the Lab does not start, so a broken Lab costs time, never a bad pull request.

lab.title: Back up n8n and prove it with a restore
needs: About 400 MB of disk for the n8n and gitleaks images
lab.goal: Export n8n workflows into a folder the way the nightly backup will, catch a pasted token with gitleaks before it could reach GitHub, and prove the backup by restoring it into a fresh n8n.

guess.q: You restore Vanil's workflow backup into a brand-new n8n. The workflow uses a credential called Vanta API. What comes back?

options.text: The workflow and the credential, with its secret.
options.why: A workflow export holds only the credential's id and name. The secret never leaves the old n8n's database.

options.text: The workflow, pointing at a credential the new n8n does not have.
options.why: The restore brings back the nodes and their wiring. Someone must create the credential again, so the page must say where its secret comes from.

options.text: Nothing, because n8n refuses a workflow whose credential is missing.
options.why: The import works. The workflow would only fail later, when it runs and the credential is not there.

follow.say: Make a scratch folder and write a small made-up workflow shaped like Vanil's hourly sync. Its Vanta step uses a proper n8n credential.
Start n8n in Docker with the folder mounted at /lab, and import the workflow, as if this were the n8n where Vanil lives today. The first run downloads the image.
follow.do:
docker run -d --name n8n-lab -v "$PWD":/lab -e N8N_DIAGNOSTICS_ENABLED=false -e N8N_ENFORCE_SETTINGS_FILE_PERMISSIONS=true docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:1.123.4
sleep 15 && docker exec n8n-lab n8n import:workflow --input=/lab/vanil-sync.json | tail -1
follow.see:
edc839860aafd89771f16e5b7405b09bdd4399b0e6555f76d790e41fc014b2fb
Successfully imported 1 workflow.
(your container id is different; the first run also downloads the image)

follow.say: A teammate also built a second workflow in a hurry, and pasted a GitHub token straight into a header. Import it too.
Take the backup: export every workflow, one file each, into the folder that would become the git repo. Then look at how the sync workflow's credential appears.
follow.do:
docker exec n8n-lab n8n export:workflow --all --pretty --separate --output=/lab/backup/ | tail -1
ls backup && grep -A4 '"credentials"' backup/vanilSync0000001.json

follow.say: Scan before anything could reach GitHub. --redact keeps the token itself off your screen.
follow.see:
Finding:     REDACTED
Secret:      REDACTED
RuleID:      github-pat
File:        /scan/vanilRedline0001.json
Line:        49
…
WRN leaks found: 1
exit 1

follow.say: Take the leaking file out of the backup for now (the Build step fixes it properly). Then prove the backup the only way that counts: restore it into a fresh n8n that has never seen these workflows.
follow.do:
rm backup/vanilRedline0001.json
docker run -d --name n8n-restore -v "$PWD":/lab -e N8N_DIAGNOSTICS_ENABLED=false -e N8N_ENFORCE_SETTINGS_FILE_PERMISSIONS=true docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:1.123.4
sleep 15 && docker exec n8n-restore n8n import:workflow --separate --input=/lab/backup/ | tail -1
docker exec n8n-restore n8n list:workflow | grep '|'
follow.see:
87ef44897a346562b8486cdd161d886bb78ab0fd7de5fc80b7a6845857ac9a1b
Successfully imported 1 workflow.
vanilSync0000001|Vanil: Vanta to Jira sync

follow.say: Now look for what the restore did not bring back.
follow.do: docker exec n8n-restore n8n export:credentials --all --output=/tmp/creds.json | tail -1
follow.see:
No credentials found with specified filters
(the workflow points at "Vanta API", which exists only in the old n8n)

lab.build: Fix the redline workflow properly instead of leaving it out. In policy-redlines.json, remove sendHeaders and headerParameters from the second node, and point it at a credential the way the sync workflow does: "authentication": "genericCredentialType", "genericAuthType": "httpHeaderAuth", and a credentials block with an id and the name GitHub policies. (With a real token you would also revoke it now, because it sat in n8n in plain text.) Import it into n8n-lab, export the backup again, scan until gitleaks is clean, then remove n8n-restore with docker rm -f n8n-restore, start a fresh one, and restore both workflows into it.
checks: gitleaks prints no leaks found, and the exit code is 0.
docker exec n8n-restore n8n list:workflow | grep '|' lists both vanilRedline0001 and vanilSync0000001.
backup/vanilRedline0001.json has a credentials block with only an id and a name.
lab.fix: A teammate wrote the backup's proof as docker exec n8n-lab n8n import:workflow --separate --input=/lab/backup/, followed by list:workflow, in the same n8n the backup came from. It passes. Make an empty folder with mkdir -p empty and point their test at /lab/empty/ instead: it imports 0 workflows and still lists both. Explain why their test can never fail, and show that your fresh-container restore fails on the empty folder. When you are done, remove both containers with docker rm -f n8n-lab n8n-restore.
explain: Why does a backup only count after a restore into a fresh n8n, and not into the one it came from?
A workflow export never holds a credential's secret. Why do we still scan it before the first push?
Why is a recorded walkthrough not enough to call a handover done, and what is?
lab.done: gitleaks is clean, both workflows come back in a fresh n8n, you can show why the same-container test proves nothing, and both containers are removed.

check.q: Which of these proves that the Byte handover is done?

options.text: The second maintainer shipped one real change to Byte through review, with Byte's builder reviewing but not driving, and corrected the page.
options.why: Building, testing and deploying it yourself is the only way to show you can fix it without the builder.

options.text: The walkthrough recording exists and the when-it-breaks page is written.
options.why: That is where a handover starts. Nobody has yet shown they can change and deploy Byte.

options.text: The second maintainer has write access, the alerts and the right to approve signing.
options.why: Access is needed, but it proves nothing. Many people with access could not fix the tool at night.

check.q: A teammate proves the n8n backup by importing it into the same n8n it came from and listing the workflows. What is wrong with that test?

options.text: Nothing; if the list shows the workflows, the backup works.
options.why: The list shows them because they were never deleted from that n8n. The backup played no part.

options.text: It can never fail: even an empty backup passes, because the workflows were never gone.
options.why: A proof must be able to fail. Only a restore into an n8n that has never seen the workflows shows what the backup really holds.

options.text: It should scan the backup with gitleaks instead.
options.why: The scan answers a different question, whether a secret leaked. It says nothing about whether the backup restores.

check.q: Vanil's workflow export is ready to push to its new private repo. What happens first, and why?

options.text: Push it: the repo is private and exports never hold secrets.
options.why: Exports leave proper credentials out, but a token pasted into a node's settings is exported in plain text, and private repos get cloned and shared.

options.text: Delete every credential id and name from the JSON by hand.
options.why: Ids and names are not secrets, and a restore needs them to know which credential each node uses.

options.text: Run gitleaks on the files, and push only when it is clean.
options.why: The scan catches the tokens people paste into nodes by mistake, before they reach git history, which is very hard to clean.

p: G0-04: Nave transfers fcp-local-lab to RhinoHealth as a private repo with fcp's team access and points the fcp-lab plugin at the new URL (the plugin moves into RhinoHealth/claude-plugins in G8). Vanil's workflows (the hourly Vanta to Jira sync and the policy redline job) are exported into a new private repo RhinoHealth/vanil after a gitleaks scan, and a nightly n8n workflow (Schedule Trigger, n8n node Workflows: Get many, GitHub node with a one-repo token) writes every workflow there. The proof is a restore of one workflow into a test n8n project.

G0-05 and G0-06: a second maintainer from Platform, named before the sessions, gets a recorded walkthrough of Byte (the per-PR pipeline of gate, broker, review, sniff and finalize, fix mode, config/repositories.json, build-worker.yml signing, the telemetry branch) and of FCP Lab (lab-up, seeding, per-environment isolation, lab-doctor, lab-clean), plus docs/when-it-breaks.md in each repo, write access, the #byte alerts, approval on the worker-signing environment, and review rights on Lab PRs. G0-06 also lists what G3's Packer image needs from the Lab. G0-17, in W3, is the proof: one real change under half a day in each tool, Nave reviewing but not driving, and both pages corrected.

Plan gaps found while writing this lesson: gitleaks runs only before the first push, but the nightly GitHub node writes straight to the repo, so a token pasted into a node later lands in git with no scan (add a scan step, or GitHub's push protection on RhinoHealth/vanil). A restore brings back no credentials: their secrets live only in n8n's database, encrypted with n8n's encryption key, and no ticket says where that key is kept or how Vanil's credentials are re-created after a loss. Vanil and n8n get a backup but no named second maintainer; only Byte and the Lab do.

tickets.why: Move the Lab and Vanil into the org, scan the export, back up n8n nightly, prove it with a restore.
Byte's walkthrough, its when-it-breaks page and the second maintainer's access.
FCP Lab's walkthrough and page, and what the VM image needs from the Lab.
The proof: the second maintainer ships one real change to Byte and one to the Lab.

words.plain: How many people a project can lose before nobody can keep it running. For these four tools it starts at one.
A named person who can build, test, deploy and fix a tool without the person who built it.
A short runbook for someone who did not build the tool: first look, symptoms, escalate.
n8n's JSON copy of a workflow: its nodes, wiring and settings, with credentials only as an id and a name.
A scanner that fails when files or git history contain something that looks like a key or a token.

review.q: Name the three parts of a when-it-breaks page and what goes in each.
review.a: First look: the three places to check, in order. Symptoms: what you see, the likely cause, the fix. Escalate: who to call and how urgent the failure really is.

review.q: Why must a restore test use a fresh n8n, and what will it not bring back?
review.a: In the same n8n the workflows were never gone, so the test passes even with an empty backup. A fresh n8n gets the workflows but no credentials; the page must say where their secrets come from.

review.q: What does the second maintainer do for Byte to finish the handover?
review.a: Ships one small real change through review: npm ci and npm run check, try it on a branch image, put BYTE_WORKER_IMAGE back, merge, watch the main build sign the image, and fix the page where it was wrong.

remember: A handover counts only when it has been tested: the second person ships a real change, and the backup comes back in a place it did not come from.
